candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'reveal what is omitted' with 'timing' and the wall calendar led to the stop date that is often missing from an antibiotic on the discharge prescription, shown as a calendar.
candidates.working_title: The antibiotic needs a stop date on the discharge letter
candidates.core_insight: In a large US study of adults in hospital with pneumonia, two thirds received more antibiotic days than needed, almost all the extra days came from the discharge prescription, and each extra day was linked with more side effects reported by patients.
candidates.angle: Antibiotic overuse is usually discussed as a prescribing decision on admission. This study located the excess at the point of discharge, where a course without a written total duration or end date runs on. Writing the last day as a calendar date is a small, checkable fix.
candidates.position: Every antibiotic on a discharge prescription should carry the planned last day as a calendar date and the total course length, and the discharge letter should say who reviews it if the person is not better.
claims_needing_evidence: In 6,481 medical patients with pneumonia in 43 Michigan hospitals, 67.8% received excess antibiotic treatment (cohort: Vaughn et al. 2019, abstract checked)
Antibiotics prescribed at discharge accounted for 93.2% of the excess duration (Vaughn 2019)
Not documenting the total treatment duration at discharge was associated with receiving excess treatment (Vaughn 2019)

Each excess day was associated with a 5% increase in the odds of patient-reported antibiotic-associated adverse events, and excess treatment was not associated with better outcomes (Vaughn 2019; observational, so no causal verb)
NICE guidance recommends a 5-day course for most adults with community-acquired pneumonia (NICE NG138, 2019)
UK antimicrobial stewardship guidance asks prescribers to record a review or stop date (UKHSA Start Smart then Focus, updated 2023)
The risk of Clostridioides difficile infection is higher in older people (surveillance data, e.g. UKHSA; to verify before use)
evidence_leads: Vaughn VM, Flanders SA, Snyder A, et al. Excess antibiotic treatment duration and adverse events in patients hospitalized with pneumonia: a multihospital cohort study. Ann Intern Med 2019;171:153-63. doi:10.7326/M18-3640 (abstract checked on PubMed)
NICE NG138. Pneumonia (community-acquired): antimicrobial prescribing, 2019
UKHSA. Start Smart then Focus: antimicrobial stewardship toolkit for inpatient care settings, 2023 update (unsure of year)
Spellberg B, Rice LB. Duration of antibiotic therapy: shorter is better. Ann Intern Med 2019 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Most of the extra antibiotic days in a large study of pneumonia came from the prescription written at discharge.
candidates.visual_idea: Wall-calendar graphic labelled 'Illustrative example': start date and planned last dose circled, days after it shaded as 'extra days'. Beside it, two discharge lines: 'Amoxicillin, continue' and 'Amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day, last dose evening of [date]; total 5 days'. Credit line: Vaughn et al., Ann Intern Med 2019.
candidates.pause: Doctors writing discharge prescriptions recognise the 'continue' line they wrote last week.
candidates.gain: A specific wording change backed by a large study.
candidates.follow: Teaching that finds the exact point in a process where harm accumulates.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none; E142 and E145 concern medicine reviews after discharge in general, not antibiotic duration

candidates.stimulus_use: The care home manager viewpoint and 'the first hour', with the operation 'reveal what is omitted', led to the questions a care home must answer when a resident returns from hospital, which a letter written for the GP may not address.
candidates.working_title: The four answers a care home needs before the first night
candidates.core_insight: When a resident returns from hospital, care home staff need to know how the person now moves, what they can eat and drink, which medicines are next due and at what time, and what to do if they get worse overnight, so the discharge information should answer those four questions directly.
candidates.angle: Discharge letters are usually written for the GP and organised by diagnosis. The people who take over care that evening need practical answers in a different order: moving, eating, the next dose, and the plan for deterioration.
candidates.position: Discharge information for a care home should state current mobility and transfers, current eating and drinking advice, the time of the last dose of each medicine, and an escalation plan, and it should arrive with the resident.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE recommends that discharge information is shared with the care home and other providers at the time of discharge (NICE NG27, 2015; check the exact recommendation wording)
Care home staff report receiving incomplete or late information when residents return from hospital (CQC 'Beyond barriers' 2018 or qualitative studies; to find)
Many older people leave hospital with changed ability in daily activities compared with before admission (meta-analysis: Loyd et al. 2020, used in C02)
Treatment escalation or anticipatory care plans are part of recommended information at transfer (ReSPECT or Anticipatory Care Planning guidance in Scotland; to verify)
evidence_leads: NICE NG27. Transition between inpatient hospital settings and community or care home settings for adults with social care needs, 2015

Loyd C et al. Prevalence of hospital-associated disability in older adults: a meta-analysis. J Am Med Dir Assoc 2020;21:455-61

candidates.opening_line_draft: When a resident comes back from hospital, the care home needs four answers before the first night: how she moves now, what she can eat and drink, which medicines are due next, and what to do if she gets worse.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card in four boxes, each with a drawn icon (walking frame, cup, clock with a tablet, telephone): 'How does she move now?', 'What can she eat and drink?', 'What is due next, and when?', 'If she gets worse tonight, then what?'. Footer suggests these as headings for the discharge letter.
candidates.pause: Care home nurses and managers know the evening arrival with a letter that answers none of these.
candidates.gain: Four headings that make a discharge letter usable by the people providing care that night.
candidates.follow: Practical help across the hospital and care home boundary.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E027 (write the suspected dementia diagnosis in the discharge letter) and E149 (a baseline page above the bed); this concerns the practical handover to a care home. Also near C16-22 (transfer bag) and C03-08 (hip fracture return) in this collection; this is general and about letter content.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'test a familiar slogan against the evidence' with the doctor in training viewpoint led to a bed-rest slogan often repeated to new staff, checked against the studies usually linked to it.
candidates.working_title: Ten days in bed, ten years of ageing: what was measured
candidates.core_insight: The slogan that ten days in a hospital bed ages an older person's muscles by ten years points in the right direction, but the best-known bed-rest study measured something narrower: in 11 healthy volunteers with an average age of 67, ten days of continuous bed rest reduced leg strength and aerobic capacity substantially, while simple physical performance tests did not change.
candidates.angle: The slogan is useful for motivation and loose as a fact. Quoting what was actually measured (strength, stair-climbing power, aerobic capacity, in healthy people lying in bed for ten days) is more accurate, still alarming, and harder to dismiss.
candidates.position: Teach the measured findings rather than the slogan; the case for getting older people up and moving in hospital is strong enough without an equivalence nobody measured directly (the last clause needs checking before use).
claims_needing_evidence: In 11 healthy older adults (mean age 67) on 10 days of continuous bed rest, knee extensor strength fell by 13.2%, stair-climbing power by 14% and maximal aerobic capacity by 12%, while SPPB and a five-item physical performance test did not change significantly (Kortebein et al. 2008, abstract checked)
The same group lost about 1 kg of lean leg mass (Kortebein et al. 2007 JAMA research letter; full text needed)

The slogan 'for people over 80, 10 days in hospital leads to the equivalent of 10 years of muscle ageing' is used in NHS campaigns such as End PJ Paralysis and attributed to Gill et al. 2004 (campaign materials; to find the exact source and wording)
Gill et al. 2004 studied the link between hospitalisation, restricted activity and new disability in community-living older people, and did not measure muscle ageing (read the Gill 2004 abstract)
Low mobility during hospital stays is associated with functional decline in older people (cohort: Brown CJ et al. 2004 J Am Geriatr Soc; to check)
evidence_leads: Kortebein P, Symons TB, Ferrando A, et al. Functional impact of 10 days of bed rest in healthy older adults. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2008;63:1076-81. doi:10.1093/gerona/63.10.1076 (abstract checked on PubMed)

Gill TM, Allore HG, Holford TR, Guo Z. Hospitalization, restricted activity, and the development of disability among older persons. JAMA 2004;292:2115-24 (PubMed record found)
End PJ Paralysis campaign materials, 2017 onwards (unsure of the exact citation used)
Brown CJ, Friedkin RJ, Inouye SK. Prevalence and outcomes of low mobility in hospitalized older patients. J Am Geriatr Soc 2004;52:1263-70 (unsure of pages)
candidates.opening_line_draft: The saying that ten days in a hospital bed ages the muscles by ten years is widely taught; the study usually linked to it measured something narrower, and still worrying.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card. Left, the slogan in quotation marks with the label 'What is often said'. Right, 'What was measured': 11 healthy volunteers, average age 67, 10 days of bed rest; three bars for knee strength, stair-climbing power and aerobic capacity with the measured falls; a fourth line 'Simple physical performance tests: no significant change'. Credit line: Kortebein et al., J Gerontol A 2008.
candidates.pause: Staff who have repeated the slogan at an induction will want to know what sits behind it.
candidates.gain: The actual figures to quote, and the limits of the study.
candidates.follow: Careful reading of the evidence behind popular claims, without dismissing the underlying concern.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E131 (bed rest is a frailty accelerator; a week in bed can take more muscle than a year of ordinary ageing) made a similar equivalence claim; this post examines the evidence behind such claims. candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'look at the smallest practical detail' with the community pharmacist viewpoint, 'the first night' and 'unpacking' led to the doses already given on the day of discharge and the day a weekly medicine is next due, checked as the bag is unpacked at home.
candidates.working_title: Which of today's doses have you already had?
candidates.core_insight: On the day you leave hospital, ask which of that day's doses the ward has already given and when each medicine is next due, including any weekly tablet or patch, so that nothing is doubled or missed on the first evening at home.
candidates.angle: Discharge advice focuses on which medicines changed. The first evening depends on something smaller: the ward may have given the morning and lunchtime doses, and a weekly tablet's day may have moved during the admission.
candidates.position: Discharge information should state the time of the last dose given on the ward for each medicine and the next due day for weekly medicines; families are entitled to ask for it.
claims_needing_evidence: Medication errors and discrepancies are common in the period after discharge from hospital (systematic review: Alqenae et al. 2020)
Taking a weekly medicine such as methotrexate daily by mistake can cause serious harm, and UK regulators have issued safety measures about it (MHRA Drug Safety Update, September 2020)
Weekly bisphosphonates such as alendronate are taken on a fixed day each week (product information)
Hospitals usually supply medicines to take home at discharge, and the ward may have given that day's earlier doses (describe as general practice; check wording with a pharmacy source)

candidates.opening_line_draft: On the day you leave hospital, ask which of today's tablets you have already been given.

candidates.follow: Concrete, low-effort actions for families at a stressful moment.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'trace a handover between people or services' and 'rationing' led to following a home care package from the day of admission, through suspension or release, to the restart that discharge depends on.
candidates.working_title: Is the home care being kept open?
candidates.core_insight: If someone had home carers before going into hospital, the family can ask early whether that care is being held open and for how long, because care that is released during the admission may have to be arranged again before discharge.
candidates.angle: Families assume the carers will simply restart. The handover between hospital and home care provider is a separate step, and its timing is set by local rules the family rarely hears about.
candidates.position: Families should be told on admission what happens to an existing home care package and for how long it is held, and should ask if they are not told.
claims_needing_evidence: Home care packages may be suspended during a hospital stay and may be ended if the stay goes beyond a locally set period (local authority or provider policies; ADASS or Healthwatch reports; to find)
Waiting for home care to start or restart is one of the recorded reasons for delayed discharge (Public Health Scotland delayed discharge statistics reason codes; NHS England discharge delay data)
Older people whose discharge is delayed spend extra days in hospital (NAO 2016; Rojas-Garcia et al. 2018)

National Audit Office. Discharging older patients from hospital, 2016

candidates.opening_line_draft: If carers came to your mother's home before she went into hospital, ask whether that care is being kept open for her, and until when.
candidates.visual_idea: Simple timeline diagram labelled 'Illustrative sequence': admission day; home care provider told; care held for a set period (period shown as 'set locally'); care released or kept; discharge date; care restarts or a new package is sought. A question mark at each handover with the question to ask.

candidates.gain: A question to ask on day one rather than at discharge.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Residue' suggested the test results left over after discharge, the ward clerk viewpoint suggested results arriving after the patient has gone, and the operation 'ask who bears the cost' pointed to the patient and GP who inherit a result that nobody owns.
candidates.working_title: Results still awaited: name who will read them
candidates.core_insight: Many patients leave hospital with test results still to come back, and in a US study the responsible doctors were unaware of most of the potentially actionable ones, so every discharge letter should list the awaited results and name who will act on them.
candidates.angle: The cost of an unowned result falls on the patient, who may not know a test was sent, and on the GP, who receives it without context. The fix is a named person and a line on the letter.
candidates.position: A discharge letter should list tests still awaited and name the person responsible for acting on each; 'GP to chase' without saying what or why moves the risk without managing it.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 2,644 patients discharged from two US academic hospitals in 2004, 41% had test results return after discharge (cross-sectional: Roy et al. 2005, abstract checked)
9.4% of the returning results were potentially actionable, and physicians were unaware of 61.6% of those surveyed; of these, 37% were judged actionable and about 13% urgent (Roy 2005)
The study could not show whether lack of awareness led to harm (Roy 2005 limitation)
Interventions to track results pending at discharge have been evaluated with mixed effects (systematic review: Darragh et al. 2018; to check)

candidates.opening_line_draft: Test results that come back after discharge are easy to miss: in a US study, the responsible doctors were unaware of most of the potentially actionable ones.

Below, a mock discharge-letter box headed 'Results awaited: test, expected date, who will act'.

candidates.gain: A one-line addition to the discharge letter that closes a known gap.
candidates.follow: Specific fixes to handovers between hospital and primary care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare the stated aim of a service with what happens', with 'delay', the GP viewpoint and 'the last week of life', led to rapid discharge home to die, whose aim is speed and whose steps can each wait on another.
candidates.working_title: Getting home to die: start every step on the same day
candidates.core_insight: When a person who is dying wants to go home and time is short, the discharge depends on several separate arrangements (equipment, medicines for symptoms, community nurses, the GP, care overnight and transport), and asking for them all to be started the same day gives the best chance of getting home in time.
candidates.angle: A 'rapid discharge' is only as fast as its slowest step. Families can ask what each step is waiting for, and the GP and district nurses need to know on the day, not from a letter afterwards.
candidates.position: Rapid discharge to die at home should run its steps in parallel, with one named coordinator, and families should be told openly that time may run out (judgement).
claims_needing_evidence: Quality improvement work on rapid (compassionate) discharge identifies delays in obtaining home equipment and medicines and poor communication between teams as the main barriers (BMJ Open Qual 2024 'Fulfilling last wishes'; read full text)
NICE recommends anticipatory prescribing of medicines for likely symptoms in the last days of life (NICE NG31, 2015)

In England, the NHS Continuing Healthcare Fast Track Pathway allows care to be funded quickly for people nearing the end of life (DHSC National Framework for NHS Continuing Healthcare, 2022); check the Scottish equivalent before use
Some people referred for rapid discharge die in hospital before discharge can happen (service audits or studies; to find)

candidates.opening_line_draft: When someone who is dying wants to go home, ask the ward to start every part of the discharge today, and ask what each part is waiting for.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'ask what would change the decision' with the spouse viewpoint led to the admission decision in the emergency department, where what the family can and can't provide at home is part of the decision.
candidates.working_title: What would let him be treated at home tonight?
candidates.core_insight: In the emergency department, the decision to admit an older person partly depends on what support is available at home, so it is reasonable to ask what would need to be in place for treatment at home, and to say clearly what you can and can't provide.
candidates.angle: Families often feel the admission decision is purely medical. Asking what would change it brings in services such as hospital at home or urgent community response where they exist, and it also protects a spouse from silently taking on more than they can manage.
candidates.position: Staff should ask families both what they can offer and what they can't, and families should feel free to say either; neither answer should be assumed (judgement).
claims_needing_evidence: For selected older people referred for admission, hospital-level care at home with comprehensive geriatric assessment had similar outcomes to admission (RCT: Shepperd et al. 2021)
Urgent community response services in England aim to respond to people in crisis at home within two hours (NHS England, 2022; check)
Availability of hospital at home and same-day community services varies by area (Healthcare Improvement Scotland Hospital at Home programme; NHS England virtual wards; to verify)
Many older people prefer to be treated at home when it is safe (survey or trial satisfaction data; Shepperd 2021 secondary outcomes)

NHS England. Urgent community response: two-hour standard guidance, 2022 (unsure)
Healthcare Improvement Scotland. Hospital at Home programme reports (unsure)
British Geriatrics Society. Silver Book II: quality care for older people with urgent care needs, 2021
candidates.opening_line_draft: In the emergency department, you can ask what would need to be in place for your husband to be treated at home tonight rather than admitted.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card with two columns under the heading 'Tell the team': 'What we can do tonight' and 'What we can't do', with example rows drawn as blank lines (for example 'stay overnight', 'help him to the toilet', 'give tablets', 'lift him if he falls'), and a third box 'Ask: is there a hospital at home or rapid response team here?'.
candidates.pause: A spouse sitting beside a trolley at midnight wonders whether home is possible.
candidates.gain: A question that opens alternatives and a way to state limits without guilt.
candidates.follow: Supports families without assuming unlimited unpaid care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E116 (tell the team who this person was last week) concerns baseline; this concerns the admission decision. Near C17-02 in this collection, which applies a similar question to discharge rather than admission.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Weather forecasting' and 'exceptions' suggested prediction and the people a forecast misses; the operation 'change the viewpoint' moved attention from the score to what the person and family know that the score leaves out.
candidates.working_title: What a readmission risk score can't see
candidates.core_insight: A systematic review found that most readmission risk prediction models discriminate poorly, and few include function or social circumstances, which the person and their family can often describe at the bedside.
candidates.angle: Scores are often used to decide who gets extra discharge support. The review shows their limits and suggests the missing information is the kind a conversation provides: who is at home, whether medicines can be managed, how the person walked before.
candidates.position: Use readmission scores as a prompt at most, and ask the person and family the questions the score leaves out before deciding who needs extra support.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 26 validated readmission models, those based on administrative data tested in large US populations had poor discrimination (c statistic 0.55 to 0.65) (systematic review: Kansagara et al. 2011, abstract checked)
Models usable early in admission had c statistics of 0.56 to 0.72, and those usable at discharge 0.68 to 0.83 (Kansagara 2011)
Few models examined function, illness severity or social determinants; two studies found functional and social variables improved discrimination (Kansagara 2011)
A plain reading of the c statistic: the chance that the model ranks a randomly chosen readmitted patient above one who was not readmitted, where 0.5 is chance (methods source)
Later reviews reached similar conclusions (Zhou et al. 2016 BMJ Open; to check)
evidence_leads: Kansagara D, Englander H, Salanitro A, et al. Risk prediction models for hospital readmission: a systematic review. JAMA 2011;306:1688-98. doi:10.1001/jama.2011.1515 (abstract checked on PubMed)
Zhou H, Della PR, Roberts P, Goh L, Dhaliwal SS. Utility of models to predict 28-day or 30-day unplanned hospital readmissions: an updated systematic review. BMJ Open 2016;6:e011060 (unsure)
van Walraven C et al. Derivation and validation of an index to predict early death or unplanned readmission after discharge from hospital to the community (LACE). CMAJ 2010;182:551-7 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Most readmission risk scores rank patients only modestly better than chance, and few include what the person's family could tell you.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a scale from 0.5 ('no better than chance') to 1.0 ('perfect ranking') with the reported ranges of c statistics marked as bands and labelled by model type; beside it, a short list 'Often missing from the models': walking before admission, who is at home, managing medicines, understanding of the plan. Credit line: Kansagara et al., JAMA 2011.
candidates.pause: Discharge coordinators who use a risk score every day will want to know how well it works.
candidates.gain: A calibrated view of the score and the questions to add.
candidates.follow: Evidence reading that respects both tools and conversations.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare what is recorded with what is experienced' and 'queuing' led to comparing the points at which official waiting-time clocks start with the wait a person experiences from arrival, or from the 999 call.
candidates.working_title: When does the waiting clock start?
candidates.core_insight: Different official emergency waiting measures start their clocks at different points, so a person's experienced wait, from the call or arrival to a ward bed, can be much longer than a headline figure suggests; knowing which clock a figure uses helps readers interpret it.
candidates.angle: The '12-hour trolley wait' in England has been counted from the decision to admit, while research linking long waits with harm, such as the 2022 English mortality study, measured from arrival. Two figures with similar names describe different waits.
candidates.position: explanatory, no position
claims_needing_evidence: NHS England's '12-hour trolley wait' measure counts time from decision to admit to admission (NHS England A&E statistics definitions; official document needed)
NHS England also publishes, or has published, the number of patients spending 12 hours or more in A&E from arrival (NHS England statistics; check dates)
Public Health Scotland reports A&E waits measured from arrival to departure (PHS A&E activity and waiting times; check)
Time waiting in an ambulance outside the department before handover may not be counted in A&E time (NHS England or ambulance service definitions; check)
The Jones et al. 2022 mortality study measured time from arrival at the emergency department (abstract checked)

candidates.working_title: A fall from standing height can be major trauma
candidates.core_insight: In UK trauma registry data, falls from less than two metres became the commonest cause of major trauma, and older people make up a large share of major trauma patients, so a low fall in an older person should be assessed for serious injury rather than triaged by mechanism alone.
candidates.angle: Trauma systems were designed around road collisions in young people. For older people the mechanism looks minor while the injury can be severe, especially rib fractures, where each additional fracture is linked with higher risk of pneumonia and death.
candidates.position: Triage of older people after a fall should look at the injury and the person (age, anticoagulants, rib and head injury) rather than the height of the fall.
claims_needing_evidence: In TARN data, the mean age of major trauma patients rose from 36.1 in 1990 to 53.8 in 2013, people over 75 were 26.9% of cases in 2013, and falls from less than 2 m were the commonest mechanism (39.1%) (registry analysis: Kehoe et al. 2015, abstract checked)

candidates.working_title: Hospital at home: what the UK trial found
candidates.core_insight: In a UK trial of 1,055 older people referred for emergency admission, treatment by a hospital-at-home team with comprehensive geriatric assessment gave similar rates of living at home and of death at six months as hospital admission, and fewer people were in long-term residential care.
candidates.angle: The default assumes hospital is safest. For selected, stable older people, the trial suggests home treatment can match it on the main outcomes, with fewer moves into care homes; what it asks of families and how people were selected need to be stated too.
candidates.position: For selected older people who are medically unwell but stable, hospital-level care at home with a geriatric team is a reasonable alternative to admission; the choice should include what the person wants and what the household can manage.
claims_needing_evidence: At 6 months, 78.6% of the hospital-at-home group and 75.3% of the hospital group were living at home (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.15) (RCT: Shepperd et al. 2021, abstract checked)

candidates.working_title: Count the bed moves
candidates.core_insight: Hospitals report admissions and length of stay but rarely the number of times one person is moved between beds and wards, although an Australian hospital study found each move was linked with higher odds of an injurious fall.
candidates.angle: Each move means a new bay, new staff and a new handover, and for an older person often a night of disruption. The number of moves is easy to count and seldom reported.
candidates.position: Hospitals should count bed and ward moves per patient, report moves at night, and avoid moves of older people for bed management reasons where possible (judgement supported by observational data).
claims_needing_evidence: In 14,133 patients in one Australian hospital in 2008 to 2009, each bed or ward transfer was associated with increased odds of falls with injury and of wound infections in surgical patients; medication errors were not associated (cross-sectional: Blay et al. 2017, abstract checked)

Routine NHS statistics do not report the number of bed moves per patient (check PHS and NHS England publications; phrase cautiously)
Night-time moves of patients are recorded by some hospitals and have been reported through freedom of information requests (to find a published source or drop)

candidates.working_title: Longer waits for a bed, more deaths within 30 days
candidates.core_insight: In English hospital data covering over five million admitted patients, longer time in the emergency department before admission was linked with higher 30-day mortality after adjustment for age, illness and crowding, rising steadily from about five hours after arrival.
candidates.angle: The study is often summarised as 'one extra death for every 82 patients delayed'. Reading it properly means saying what it adjusted for, that it is observational, and that the figure describes patients waiting beyond 6 to 8 hours compared with shorter waits.
candidates.position: Long waits before admission are a patient-safety problem and should be reported as one; the study shows a consistent link, not proof that each extra hour causes a death.
claims_needing_evidence: The study included 5,249,891 patients admitted from type 1 emergency departments in England from April 2016 to March 2018 (cross-sectional: Jones et al. 2022, abstract checked)
Mortality rose in a linear fashion from 5 hours after arrival up to 12 hours (Jones 2022)
The authors estimated one extra death for every 82 admitted patients whose transfer to a bed was delayed beyond 6 to 8 hours from arrival (Jones 2022; check the comparison group in the full text)
The model adjusted for sex, age, deprivation, comorbidities, time of day, month, previous attendances and department crowding (Jones 2022)
Older people are more likely than younger adults to experience long emergency department waits (NHS England, PHS or RCEM data; to find)

candidates.working_title: On a trolley for hours: the basics still apply
candidates.core_insight: During a long wait on a trolley or chair in the emergency department, an older person still needs a drink if allowed, help to the toilet, their usual medicines on time, and help to change position, and it is reasonable to ask for each.
candidates.angle: Long waits are discussed as a system failure. For the person on the trolley, the harms are specific and partly preventable: missed doses, pressure damage, thirst and incontinence from not being taken to the toilet. Naming them helps families ask kindly and precisely.
candidates.position: Basic care during a long wait is part of treatment, and asking for it is reasonable; staff working in crowded departments are not the problem this post describes.
claims_needing_evidence: Pressure ulcers occur in emergency departments, and longer stays in the department are associated with their occurrence (prospective study: Dugaret et al. 2012, Int Wound J; read the abstract)

candidates.working_title: A normal temperature can be a fever for this person
candidates.core_insight: Older people with serious infection often do not reach standard fever thresholds, so a rise from the person's usual temperature (such as an increase of more than 1.1 degrees Celsius) or a lower repeated threshold can indicate infection even when an early warning score records the temperature as normal.
candidates.angle: NEWS2 gives no points for temperatures from 36.1 to 38.0 degrees. For an older person whose usual temperature is around 36.0, a reading of 37.5 may be a meaningful change that the score does not flag. The practical step is to record and compare with the person's baseline.
candidates.position: When assessing an older person for infection, compare the temperature with their usual reading, and do not let a 'normal' temperature or a low early warning score close the question.
claims_needing_evidence: The IDSA guideline for long-term care residents defines fever as a single oral temperature above 37.8 degrees C, repeated oral readings above 37.2 degrees C, or an increase of more than 1.1 degrees C over baseline (High et al. 2009; check the full text for exact wording)

Older adults may have lower baseline temperatures and blunted fever responses (review: Norman 2000 Clin Infect Dis; to check)
The guideline population was long-term care residents, not all older people in emergency departments (state as a limitation)

candidates.working_title: What comprehensive geriatric assessment does in hospital
candidates.core_insight: Across 29 trials, older people who received comprehensive geriatric assessment (a full assessment of health, function, medicines, mood and support by a specialist team) after admission were more likely to be alive and living in their own homes 3 to 12 months later, with little or no difference in deaths and fewer moves into care homes.
candidates.angle: The benefit shows up in an outcome patients value, living at home, rather than in survival. Whether a dedicated ward works better than a visiting team is often asserted, but the latest Cochrane review says the evidence is too weak to tell.
candidates.position: Older people with frailty admitted as emergencies should have access to comprehensive geriatric assessment; claims about which delivery model is best should be made cautiously.
claims_needing_evidence: 29 trials with 13,766 participants were included (Cochrane review: Ellis et al. 2017, abstract checked)

Little or no difference in mortality (RR 1.00) and fewer nursing home admissions (RR 0.80) (Ellis 2017)
The review was uncertain whether wards and mobile teams differ, because the analysis was underpowered (Ellis 2017)

candidates.working_title: What discharge planning achieves in trials
candidates.core_insight: In a Cochrane review of 33 trials, an individual discharge plan for older people admitted with a medical condition probably shortened the initial stay by less than a day and modestly reduced readmissions over about three months, with little or no difference in mortality or function.
candidates.angle: Discharge planning is universally recommended and often presented as the answer to delays. The trial evidence supports it with modest effects, which is useful for setting expectations and for seeing what else discharge depends on.
candidates.position: Individual discharge planning is worth doing and its benefits are modest; it should be judged by realistic expectations rather than as a solution to every delay.
claims_needing_evidence: 33 trials with 12,242 participants were included (Cochrane review: Gonçalves-Bradley et al. 2022, abstract checked)

candidates.working_title: 'Medically fit' needs a second sentence
candidates.core_insight: 'Medically fit for discharge' records that acute medical treatment is finished, and the note should also say what the person still needs, such as rehabilitation, a care package, equipment or a result, because many older people are less able at that point than before they became ill.
candidates.angle: The phrase is a common shortcut. It is read by families and other teams as 'well' or 'back to normal', and it can make the remaining needs look like somebody else's problem. A second sentence fixes both.
candidates.position: Write 'no longer needs acute medical care' and follow it with the person's remaining needs and who is meeting them; explain the phrase to families when it is used.
claims_needing_evidence: About 3 in 10 older adults leave acute hospital with new loss of independence in at least one basic daily activity (meta-analysis: Loyd et al. 2020)

candidates.working_title: Delayed discharge is counted in bed days
candidates.core_insight: Delayed discharge is reported mainly as bed days, a measure of the hospital's capacity, while a mixed-studies review found it is linked with infections, depression, loss of mobility and daily activities, and death for the person who is waiting.
candidates.angle: The official count describes the hospital's problem. The person's problem is different and is not in the headline. The phrase 'bed blocker' places the fault on the person who is waiting for services to be arranged.
candidates.position: Reports on delayed discharge should describe what waiting does to the person as well as the bed days lost, and the term 'bed blocker' should not be used (judgement).
claims_needing_evidence: Delayed discharge was associated with mortality, infections, depression, and reductions in mobility and daily activities; most quantitative studies were of moderate or low quality (systematic review: Rojas-Garcia et al. 2018, abstract checked)

candidates.working_title: Sent home from A&E: ask about the next step
candidates.core_insight: Older people who go home from the emergency department have higher rates of return visits, admission and loss of function in the following months than younger adults, so before leaving it helps to ask what was found, what should prompt a return, and whether any follow-up has been arranged.
candidates.angle: Going home from A&E feels like good news and often is. The evidence says it is also a point of risk for older people, particularly those who live alone or were already struggling, and a few questions make the next weeks safer.
candidates.position: Older people leaving the emergency department should leave with a clear reason to return and, where needed, a referral (for example after a fall); families can ask for both.
claims_needing_evidence: Compared with younger people, older adults have longer emergency department stays, more repeat visits and higher rates of adverse outcomes after discharge (systematic review: Aminzadeh and Dalziel 2002, abstract checked)
Risk factors include functional impairment, recent hospital or emergency use, living alone and lack of social support (Aminzadeh and Dalziel 2002)

candidates.working_title: How many readmissions are avoidable? Studies disagree widely
candidates.core_insight: A systematic review of 34 studies found that the proportion of readmissions judged avoidable ranged from 5% to 79%, with a median of about 27%, mostly using subjective judgements at single hospitals, so a readmission rate on its own says little about the quality of a discharge.
candidates.angle: Readmission rates are used as quality indicators. If most readmissions are unavoidable, and studies can't agree how many are, the rate mixes good and poor care. Reviewing a sample of readmissions for specific preventable causes tells a team more.
candidates.position: Treat a readmission rate as a prompt to review cases, not as a verdict on a discharge; judge discharge quality with case review and outcomes people value (judgement grounded in the review).
claims_needing_evidence: Across 34 studies, the median proportion of readmissions deemed avoidable was 27.1%, ranging from 5% to 79% (systematic review: van Walraven et al. 2011, abstract checked)
All but three studies used subjective criteria; most were at single teaching hospitals, used one reviewer and did not consider community information (van Walraven 2011)
Later national cohort work in US general medicine found about a quarter of readmissions potentially preventable (Auerbach et al. 2016 JAMA Intern Med; to check)
Some reviews question whether readmission rate is a valid quality indicator (Fischer et al. 2014 PLoS One; to check)

Auerbach AD, Kripalani S, Vasilevskis EE, et al. Preventability and causes of readmissions in a national cohort of general medicine patients. JAMA Intern Med 2016;176:484-93 (unsure of pages)
Fischer C, Lingsma HF, Marang-van de Mheen PJ, et al. Is the readmission rate a valid quality indicator? A review of the evidence. PLoS One 2014;9:e112282 (unsure)

candidates.working_title: Pneumonia in a care home: hospital, or treatment where they live?
candidates.core_insight: In a Canadian trial in 22 nursing homes, residents with pneumonia treated in the home on a clinical pathway (oral antibiotics, oxygen monitoring, fluids and close nursing review) were admitted to hospital less than half as often as those given usual care, without a clear difference in deaths.
candidates.angle: The choice is often presented as hospital or nothing. The trial shows a third option that worked when the home had extra monitoring. The decision still depends on the person's wishes, how unwell they are, and what the home can provide.
candidates.position: For care home residents with pneumonia, treatment in the home with proper monitoring is a reasonable option for many, and the decision should include the resident's wishes and the home's capacity to monitor (judgement based on one trial).
claims_needing_evidence: In 680 residents aged 65 and over in 22 Ontario nursing homes, 10% of the pathway group and 22% of the usual care group were hospitalised (cluster RCT: Loeb et al. 2006, abstract checked)
Mortality was 8% versus 9% with no clear difference; quality of life and function did not differ (Loeb 2006)
The pathway included oral antibiotics, portable chest X-ray, oxygen saturation monitoring, rehydration and close monitoring by a research nurse (Loeb 2006)
UK care homes may not have equivalent nursing or monitoring, so applicability varies (state as limitation)
evidence_leads: Loeb M, Carusone SC, Goeree R, et al. Effect of a clinical pathway to reduce hospitalizations in nursing home residents with pneumonia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA 2006;295:2503-10. doi:10.1001/jama.295.21.2503 (abstract checked on PubMed)

candidates.working_title: Ask for the planned discharge date early
candidates.core_insight: Many hospitals set an expected date of discharge early in a stay, and asking for it, and for what has to happen before it, lets families plan transport, time off work, the home and support, rather than hearing about discharge on the day.
candidates.angle: Families often learn about discharge late. The expected date is usually already written somewhere. Asking for it early, as a planning estimate that can change, turns a surprise into a plan.
candidates.position: Families should be told the expected discharge date and what it depends on, and should ask if they are not told.
claims_needing_evidence: NHS patient flow guidance recommends that every patient has an expected discharge date set early in the admission (NHS Improvement SAFER patient flow bundle, 2016 onwards; check wording)
Patients and families have reported being given little notice of discharge (Healthwatch England 'Safely home' 2015; CQC Adult Inpatient Survey discharge questions)
Individual discharge planning modestly reduces length of stay and readmission (Cochrane: Gonçalves-Bradley 2022)
Carers have a right to be involved in discharge planning in some UK legislation (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016 section 28; Care Act 2014 guidance; check, and avoid duplicating C18-16)

candidates.working_title: Older people with a learning disability in hospital
candidates.core_insight: People with a learning disability die on average many years younger than the rest of the population, and more of their deaths are judged avoidable with good health care, so a hospital stay should include the adjustments the law requires, such as a hospital passport, the learning disability liaison team and the people who know them best.
candidates.angle: People with a learning disability are now living into older age, with the frailty and illnesses that brings, and often reach geriatric wards. The confidential inquiry found problems such as not adjusting care as needs changed and carers not feeling listened to.
candidates.position: Every admission of a person with a learning disability should use their hospital passport, involve the liaison team, and include the family or support workers who know them; hospitals have a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments.
claims_needing_evidence: In the Confidential Inquiry (south-west England, deaths 2010 to 2012), the median age at death of people with intellectual disabilities was 64; men died 13 years and women 20 years younger than the general population (population study: Heslop et al. 2014, abstract checked)
37% of deaths were from causes amenable to good-quality health care, compared with 13% in the general population (Heslop 2014)
Contributory factors included problems with advance care planning, Mental Capacity Act adherence, adjusting care as needs changed and carers not feeling listened to (Heslop 2014)
More recent LeDeR reports give current median ages at death and avoidable death rates (LeDeR annual report, King's College London; check the latest year)
The Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people in services (legislation)
Learning disability liaison nurses and hospital passports are established in NHS hospitals (NHS England or professional guidance; check)

candidates.working_title: A coach for the first month after discharge
candidates.core_insight: In a US trial of 750 older people, a four-week care transitions programme that prepared patients and carers to manage their medicines, keep their own health record, arrange follow-up and recognise warning signs reduced readmissions at 30 and 90 days.
candidates.angle: The programme's effective parts are plain: it treats the patient and family as the people carrying the plan between services and gives them the skills and a named person to do it. The limitation is that the evidence comes from a US health system.
candidates.position: Discharge support should prepare the person and family to manage the first weeks themselves, with a named person to contact; UK services should test such programmes rather than assume US results transfer (judgement).
claims_needing_evidence: In 750 community-dwelling adults aged 65 and over in Colorado (2002 to 2003), readmission at 30 days was 8.3% with the intervention versus 11.9% with usual care, and at 90 days 16.7% versus 22.5% (RCT: Coleman et al. 2006, abstract checked)
The intervention included tools for cross-site communication, encouragement to take an active role and assert preferences, and a transition coach (Coleman 2006)
Readmissions for the original condition were also lower at 90 and 180 days, and hospital costs were lower at 180 days (Coleman 2006)
The four elements (medicines self-management, a personal health record, follow-up, knowledge of warning signs) are described in the programme materials (Care Transitions Program; check the full text)
Other transitional care trials, such as nurse-led discharge planning and home follow-up, also reduced readmissions (Naylor et al. 1999 JAMA; to check)
